topics.topic: When response-time session validity is evaluated and how cookie expiry avoids affecting a newer session
questions: At what instant is "no longer valid" evaluated, and how does `owner_interface` learn that a session admitted at arrival became invalid before its answer was emitted?
Is “no longer valid” evaluated when the request is admitted or when its response is produced, and how must a stale response avoid expiring a newer session cookie created meanwhile?
Is cookie expiry determined from validity at request admission, from a no_owner_session refusal, or from session validity again when the response is produced?

quotes:
On a sign-out, and on any answer to a request whose session is no
longer valid, the cookie is expired in the browser.

a request that
passed completes even if a limit or a sign-out comes while it runs (A13
rule 2).
Other open sessions stay (A13 rules 2–4).
judgement.divergence: One implementation rechecks the request's session when emitting the response and expires the browser cookie, potentially deleting a newer session cookie; another uses admission-time validity or only a `no_owner_session` refusal and leaves the cookie untouched. The owner's browser and owner observe whether the newer sign-in survives.
judgement.why: The texts require expiry for an answer whose session is no longer valid but fix neither the evaluation instant nor a response mechanism that prevents an old response from expiring a newer cookie.

witness.initial: The browser holds session S, and a slow owner read using S has passed admission.
events: The owner signs in again and the browser receives a new session cookie S2.
The admitted read using S completes and its response is emitted.
outcomes: The response uses admission-time validity and leaves S2 intact, so the next request succeeds.
The response rechecks S, expires the browser cookie, and removes S2, so the next request shows sign-in.
witness.observer: The owner's browser and the owner.
basis:
a request that
passed completes even if a limit or a sign-out comes while it runs (A13
rule 2).

On sign-in, the session cookie set: not readable by scripts, only to
Registry's origin, over HTTPS when reached from another machine (A13 rule
1).

topics.topic: Startup behavior when a leftover temporary store cannot be removed but the real store exists
questions: If the real store exists but the leftover temporary file cannot be removed, must startup fail or may it open the real store and leave the temporary file?
If a valid store exists but its leftover temporary file cannot be removed, does open_store continue with the existing store or fail the start?

judgement.why: This is the same unchanged question about an unremovable store temporary file when the real store exists.

precedent.topic: Startup behavior when a leftover store temporary file cannot be removed
quotes:
A diagnostic, and the start stops, for: a leftover it cannot remove while the
store is absent; a store that does not open, fails the check or carries
another version; a new store it cannot make, whose temporary file it
removes or, when it cannot, leaves for the next start (A17 rule 2).
precedent.why: Failure to remove the leftover is startup-fatal only while the configured store is absent, so an existing valid store is opened despite that leftover.

questions: Must a refused sign-out request expire the browser cookie when the server-side session remains valid?

quotes:
On a sign-out, and on any answer to a request whose session is no
longer valid, the cookie is expired in the browser.

A request carrying a valid session restarts its 30 minutes at its arrival,
whatever its answer — a CSRF refusal included; of concurrent arrivals the
latest counts (A13 rule 2).

The session ends; its pending confirmation and its uploaded file are
dropped (M11).
judgement.divergence: One implementation expires the cookie for every request targeting sign-out, including a CSRF-refused request; another expires it only after `sign_out_owner` accepts and ends the server session. The owner observes whether the still-valid session remains usable.
judgement.why: The phrase “On a sign-out” does not say whether it covers an attempted but refused sign-out or only an accepted sign-out operation.

witness.initial: The browser holds a valid owner session.
events: The browser submits the sign-out form with a wrong CSRF value.
`admit_owner_request` refuses the request with `csrf_refused`, leaving the server session valid.
outcomes: The surface expires the cookie because the request targeted sign-out, so the browser loses access to the live session.
The surface retains the cookie because no sign-out was accepted, so the next request remains signed in.
witness.observer: The owner and the owner's browser.
basis:
A request carrying a valid session restarts its 30 minutes at its arrival,
whatever its answer — a CSRF refusal included; of concurrent arrivals the
latest counts (A13 rule 2).

On a sign-out, and on any answer to a request whose session is no
longer valid, the cookie is expired in the browser.

questions: Does artifact history exclude the pointer's stored request id despite the promise to return every M05 fact?

quotes:
The projections an
operation's Outputs name are complete: a fact not listed there is not in
the answer.

No answer carries a request id: it is kept
with its record and never answered (A01 rule 9).

Every pointer — published, superseded, withdrawn, of removed types too —
each with every fact M05 holds: id, project, type, version, status, owner
service, `uri`, `payload_ref`, digest, publisher and published instant, the
superseded instant, the withdrawing principal and withdrawn instant; by type,
then version highest first, then pointer id.
judgement.divergence: Artifact history either omits the pointer's stored publish request id under the global convention or includes it because the operation promises every M05 fact; Client Portal observes the different response.
judgement.why: The artifact-history operation promises every fact M05 holds, which includes the publish request id, while the global convention says no answer ever carries a request id.

topics.topic: Whether expiry occurs exactly at the monotonic time limit
questions: Does the expiry pass end a session when its monotonic reading is exactly equal to a limit, or only when it is greater?

quotes:
A session that has reached a
   limit serves no request from that
   moment: a request carrying it is refused at the session check.

Each session past 8 hours or 30 minutes without a request ends, with its
pending confirmation and its uploaded file.
judgement.divergence: At a pass exactly on the deadline, one implementation ends the session and drops its upload because the limit has been reached; another retains it until the monotonic reading is greater because the operation says “past.” `instance_lifecycle` and the owner observe the different count and retained upload.
judgement.why: The earlier rule makes equality invalid by saying the limit has been reached, while the State 5 operation says the pass ends sessions only when they are past the limit.

witness.initial: An owner session has an uploaded import file and an idle deadline at monotonic reading N.
events: The expiry pass takes the import lock and the session lock at exactly N.
It evaluates whether to end the session.
outcomes: The session ends, its upload is dropped, and the returned count includes it.
The session remains until a later pass, its upload stays, and the returned count excludes it.
basis:
The pass alone ends sessions by their limits, taking the import lock and
then each session's lock and deciding under them, each session by a reading
of `clock.monotonic_reading` taken once its lock is held (A13 rule 2).

Each session past 8 hours or 30 minutes without a request ends, with its
pending confirmation and its uploaded file.
